newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian gold, coal sectors seen struggling.
newsitem.headline: Australian gold, coal sectors seen struggling.

text.p: Australia's top merchandise exports -- gold and coal -- are in trouble, hit by plunging costs and low returns that threaten the survival of some miners, an economic forecasting group said on Wednesday.
Access Economics' monthly monitor projected further falls in coal prices over the next two years and gold prices remaining stuck around current low levels.
"Both of Australia's two major export industries need to reduce costs if they are to remain healthy," Access said.

The current woes in the coal and gold sectors would also force companies to defer some of the A$11 billion worth of coal projects and A$2.5 billion worth of gold projects under construction or in planning, Access said.
Coal and gold are Australia's major merchandise exports and account for about 13 percent of all merchandise export earnings.
Coal exports were worth A$7.8 billion in 1995/96 ended June 30 and gold exports A$5.7 billion.
"Both are in trouble due to falling real prices," said Access.
It forecast gold and coking coal prices by 2000 to be 40 percent below 1980 prices, while steaming coal would be 60 percent lower than in 1980.

Access said gold production was already relatively efficient and miners could turn to mergers to maintain their viability but coal production was dogged by productivity up to 35 percent below U.S. levels.
"The coal companies have to get costs down in their existing operations to survive, let alone earn a reasonable rate of return," Access said.
Some companies are already trying to revamp existing labour conditions, while others are turning to contractors to replace employees.
Access also backed the Reserve Bank's recent sale of 167 tonnes of gold -- two thirds of its total reserves.
"... the returns from holding gold have been below the returns on bonds or inflation, so the Reserve Bank of Australia decision to sell gold is hardly surprising," Access said.
"The reaction of the gold market was less predictable given both the Canadian and South African central banks have been gold sellers and both are big gold producers.

"With large central bank gold holdings still overhanging the market, an early recovery in gold prices cannot be relied upon and Australian gold producers will need to reduce costs if they are to survive."
World gold prices have been falling steadily over the past year and hit a 12-year low last month when the Reserve Bank made public its massive sell-down.
An Access survey of economists' forecasts projected gold prices averaging US$342 an ounce in 1997 and US$354 an ounce in 1998.
Steaming coal prices are seen averaging US$37.70 a tonne in the second half of 1997 and US$37.5 a tonne in the first half of 1998, and coking coal US$54.0 and US$53.9 a tonne respectively.
